title: A strong shock wave going round a sharp corner (shock diffraction)
goal: The first flow with shocks in two dimensions. Step 2 of 7 on the way to a rotating detonation engine.
story: Solved with OpenFOAM's shock solver by a fresh agent. gpucfd's new shock solver then ran the same problem on the same grids, with its outputs read by the case's own code. Its method was picked by a rule fixed before the runs.

requirements: A square chamber of still air, 1 m by 1 m. A flat shock wave five times faster than sound enters through the upper half of the left side.
Below the opening the left side is a wall, so the shock has to bend round a sharp corner into the lower half. No friction and no heat conduction.
Asked for at 0.45 ms: the speed of the flat part of the shock and the gas behind it, whether mass and energy are kept, whether the flat part stays flat, and the pattern round the corner.
Reference: the exact jump across a shock for the flat part. The pattern round the corner has no exact solution.
Required: the flat part's speed within 0.5 % and the gas behind it within 1 %; mass and energy within 0.01 % of what flowed in; the flat part straight to within one cell.

results.headline: Completed, as expected. The three requirements are met: on 800 cells per side the flat part of the shock moves at the exact speed to within \(0.006\,\%\), the state behind it is within \(0.036\,\%\), mass and energy match the exact inflow to \(3 \times 10^{-9}\) of it, and the flat part is straight to \(6 \times 10^{-5}\) cells on every grid. gpucfd's new shock solver meets the same three requirements on the same grids, and on 800 by 800 cells it takes 16 s on the GPU against OpenFOAM's 742 s on 8 cores. Its pressure ripple behind the shock is larger: at most \(4.4\,\%\) at any written time against OpenFOAM's \(2.0\,\%\).
meaning: All three requirements are met with a wide margin. A strong shock on a grid of squares stayed flat, which some other methods are known to get wrong.
Both tools keep mass and energy and move the shock at the exact speed. On the flat part their answers agree to a few thousandths of a per cent.
gpucfd needs about 50 times less time than OpenFOAM on 8 cores for the finest common grid.

For the detonation engine: this flow needs about five time steps per cell, against two in the tube. With half as many, the gas round the corner got a negative pressure and the run broke. Eight cores gave only 2.3 times the speed of one.
limits: The speed table is not tuned on OpenFOAM's side: its runs are the solver agent's own, with a time step chosen for safety. gpucfd ran on the GPU of the same PC.
gpucfd is worse in one place: the weak waves left by the start of the shock are about twice as tall as OpenFOAM's.
The pattern round the corner is checked only against itself (two times, two grids), not against an experiment.
The start is not clean: the shock is put in as a sharp jump, and two weak waves from that start stay in the flow at about 2 % of the pressure.
answer: Both tools meet all three requirements, with a wide margin.
The flat part of the shock moves at the exact speed to within a hundredth of a per cent, and stays flat.
gpucfd is about 50 times faster on the finest grid. It is worse in one place: the weak leftover waves behind the shock are about twice as tall as OpenFOAM's.
